title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
content:
OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.
OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.
Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.
OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

report.summary: OpenAI raised $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, below its own targets, while rival Anthropic files to go public — a split in how AI's leaders approach capital markets.
report.background: The past two years have seen an unprecedented concentration of private capital in a handful of frontier AI labs, funded largely on the bet that model capability will translate into durable revenue. OpenAI's valuation has climbed steeply through successive rounds, with the company and its backers underwriting massive data center buildouts to train and serve ever-larger models. That spending has become one of the biggest capital cycles in tech history, and it increasingly depends on public market sentiment rather than pure private conviction. Meanwhile, investors have grown more demanding about timelines to profitability, energy costs, and the social footprint of AI infrastructure. The midterm elections amplified public skepticism toward AI companies and data center projects, and a pullback in tech equities has made late-stage fundraising harder even for marquee names. That backdrop explains why OpenAI is raising less than it hoped while Anthropic moves toward a public listing — two different answers to the same question of where the next dollar of growth capital comes from.
key_points: OpenAI's new round values it at $1.25 trillion with $11 billion raised, per Bloomberg, making it one of the most valuable companies in the world. It follows a March round at an $852 billion valuation — a striking jump given how short a time has passed between the two raises and how much capital is being absorbed by compute buildouts.

The round came in below OpenAI's own expectations. It had reportedly hoped to raise up to $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation and is still negotiating to push the current total toward $20 billion, suggesting investors are no longer willing to simply meet the company's asking price without pushback on terms.

Anthropic filed its S-1 last week, putting it on a path to become one of the first frontier labs to list publicly. That forces a comparison: Anthropic is opting for disclosure and public scrutiny, while OpenAI stays private and leans on a small set of deep-pocketed backers to fund its expansion.

Sam Altman framed the delay as a safety decision, saying OpenAI will hold off on an IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models' safety — while conceding it would be 'bad for the world' to wait too long. The comments position safety as both a governance stance and a negotiating posture with public markets.

Market conditions have visibly tightened. The shortfall against OpenAI's target followed a drop in tech stocks and midterm results that showed public opinion turning against AI companies and data center projects — signs that the political and financial environment around AI infrastructure is becoming less permissive.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the message is that private capital is still available but no longer unconditional: valuations remain extraordinary, yet rounds are being trimmed and terms negotiated, and the first major AI IPO will create a public benchmark that every other lab is measured against. For developers, this concentrates risk — a handful of vendors with trillion-dollar valuations have pricing power over APIs, and customers may see more tiers, usage caps, or enterprise-first feature gating as labs chase revenue. It also strengthens the case for portability across providers and for open-weight models as a hedge. For regular users, expect safety and policy work to be marketed more prominently, since it is now tied to IPO readiness and public trust, alongside continued pressure to monetize through subscriptions, ads, or enterprise deals.
report.tools: To follow the story, watch Anthropic's S-1 on SEC EDGAR for the first hard financial disclosure from a frontier lab, and OpenAI's published preparedness and safety frameworks to see how its IPO claims evolve. Crunchbase or PitchBook track the funding rounds; The Verge, Bloomberg, and the FT are breaking the numbers. For hands-on hedging against vendor concentration, evaluate open-weight models such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and DeepSeek, and compare them on LMSYS Chatbot Arena before committing to a single API.
